You describe the interface in **Contract**, a small declarative language whose layout and property names are CSS's. Make your own app ```sh bun scripts/exact.mjs new ../hello # or run `bun link` once, then `exact new ../hello` cd ../hello bun exact.mjs contract types app.contract -o app.contract.d.ts # the first run builds the compiler bun exact.mjs web # the dev loop, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ bun exact.mjs test web # the app's *.test.contract, or the files named bun exact.mjs mac --run # this Mac bun exact.mjs ios --run # an iOS Simulator ``` `exact new` creates a standalone app: `app.contract` (the view), `app.ts` (its data), `app.json` (the manifest: name, bundle id, hosts, deploy policy) and `app.test.contract` (its test). The app holds no crate: a native verb (`mac`, `ios`, `linux`, `android`, `windows`) builds in a Cargo workspace it generates under `.exact/shells/`, which uses your exact2 checkout by path. `bun exact.mjs help` lists the commands, including `bun exact.mjs contract …` for the compiler and `contract vocab` for a card of what an app writes (`--all`: every tag and property Contract accepts). Read [`docs/start-here.md`](docs/start-here.md) next, or for a website [`docs/start-here-site.md`](docs/start-here-site.md). It is the only required reading for building an app; the rest of the documentation is for lookup. The app's own `AGENTS.md` (and `CLAUDE.md`) points a coding agent at the same guide. Run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once first. Make a todo list where I can add items, check them off, delete them, and see how many are left. Put the view in Contract and keep the list in `app.ts`. Write an `app.test.contract`, pass it on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator with `scripts/agent.mjs`, then open the app for me on all three. ``` On 2026-10-04, a fresh agent given an earlier version of this prompt on a clean clone, with Hermes installed and Cargo's cache warm, finished in about 57 minutes, and its tests passed on all three platforms. About 25 of those minutes were the first macOS and iOS builds; later builds take a minute or two. ## Three principles 1. **Write the web, ship the platform.** What you write is CSS: its names, its layout model and the browser's fast development loop. What you leave out is the platform's: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, the keyboard and accessibility come out as in an app built by hand for that platform. What you write wins (LLP 1115; [details](#what-is-csss-and-what-is-the-platforms)). 2. **An agent can do the whole loop.** It can create an app, run it on any host, see it, operate it, control its clock and run its tests, with no person watching ([details](#for-agents)). 3. **Fast to start and fast to change.** The budgets below come from `rules/RULES.md`. The gate's is checked on every change and the others every hour. A regression is top priority and is attributed to the commit that caused it ([details](#how-it-stays-fast)). | Budget | Target | |---|---| | Cold start to interactive first frame | 100 ms p50 | | Dev restart, edit to present | 100 ms p50 | | App JavaScript executed before first pixel | none | | Touch one line, rebuild that crate | 30 s | | The blocking gate, warm, after a one-crate edit | 30 s | ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph author["You write"] C["app.contract
view · state · actions"] D["app.ts or a Rust crate
data sources"] end C --> K["Contract compiler"] --> P["plan
tables + bytecode"] P --> W["Web
one ES module, ~20 KB runtime,
the browser's DOM and CSS"] P --> R["Rust runner
+ layout kernel (Taffy)"] R --> M["macOS
AppKit + CoreText"] R --> I["iOS
UIKit + CoreText"] R --> L["Linux
vello GPU / tiny-skia CPU"] D -.->|answers, checked against declared shapes| W D -.-> R ``` - **Contract** (`contract/`) is compiled in four passes (syntax, types, analysis, and lowering) into a *plan*: tables and bytecode for the views, state and actions. The web build compiles the plan into its ES module; on native hosts a Rust runner executes it. At build time the plan is *baked*: constant data is evaluated into it, so the first frame needs nothing else. - **The runner** (`runner/`) is the plan's virtual machine. It handles keyed component instances, events, timers on a seekable clock, and the data seam: the one boundary where data enters the plan. - **The kernel** (`kernel/`) is a columnar node arena with CSS layout through a patched [Taffy](vendor/taffy/EXACT-PATCHES.md). The host measures text: CoreText on Apple, cosmic-text on Linux. On the web, the browser lays out the same CSS itself, so the web build carries no layout engine. - **Hosts** (`host/`) present the tree. The web host writes DOM nodes, and the browser runs CSS transitions. The Apple host is a static library with a C ABI under AppKit and UIKit presenters. The Linux host paints the tree itself, onto DRM/KMS with evdev input, or into an offscreen buffer. - **Data sources** sit below the data seam. TypeScript runs on Hermes on native hosts and in the browser's own engine on the web. Rust runs natively, and can be replaced live (as a shared library, or as Wasm on iOS and the web). A source that is one HTTP request can be declared in Contract instead; an app whose sources are all declared links no JavaScript engine on native hosts. Every answer is checked against the shape Contract declared. Grants control network, files, SQLite, and secrets. - **Optional pieces** are separate artifacts: a wgpu GPU module (Metal on Apple, WebGPU in the browser), native modules (a hyphenated tag backed by a platform widget, like MapKit), and a [game engine](game/README.md) add-on. ### What is CSS's, and what is the platform's The order of precedence is the author, then the platform, then CSS's default. One test settles a dispute: would someone who knows the platform notice the difference? If so, the platform's answer wins. - Layout is CSS's, because a person can't see a layout default, only its result. A bare node is `display: block`, `box-sizing: content-box`, `flex-direction: row`, `flex-shrink: 1`, the same as a bare `
`. - Names are CSS's, because names are what you write: `font-size`, `object-fit`, `text-overflow`, `line-clamp`, `light-dark()`, `env(safe-area-inset-top)`. The compiler refuses an alias and names the web's spelling. - Presentation you leave unsaid is the platform's. Text is the system's label colour and size (17 points on an iPhone, 13 on a Mac, the reader's setting in a browser), a `button` is the system's button, and a pushed screen has the system's Back. An app that says less looks more at home. - The browser is the reference for layout and for what you wrote. Native layout given the same inputs, Canvas 2D, SVG, gradients, and authored motion are checked against what Chrome draws. - The web is also the development loop. You work in the seconds-long web loop, and the native hosts are checked behind you. - Any unavoidable deviation in layout is declared, with its reason, in LLP 1001. For example, Taffy has no `position: static`. Writing the web doesn't mean the lowest common denominator. Where a platform can do more (real HTML in an SVG `foreignObject` on the web, MapKit through a native module on Apple), Exact lets it. ### How it stays fast - **The boot path executes and compiles nothing.** TypeScript is compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time and loads after the first pixel. { ...t, done } : t)); return { count: todos.length }; }, removeTodo: ([id]) => { todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id); return { count: todos.length }; }, }; export const answer: Answer = (source, args, store, storage, native) => sources[source](args, store, storage, native); ``` ```contract-test // app.test.contract: runs on any host with `scripts/agent.mjs --test` test "add, finish and delete" expect text "count" == "0 left" type "new-todo" "Buy milk" tap "add" type "new-todo" "Walk the dog" type "new-todo" key "Enter" expect text "count" == "2 left" tap "toggle-1" expect text "count" == "1 left" tap "remove-1" expect tree missing "todo-1" expect tree has "todo-2" ```
